newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOCUS ON RAND AFTER NEW LOW ON DLR.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOCUS ON RAND AFTER NEW LOW ON DLR.

text.p: South African financial markets begin the week in the wake of the rand's slide to its lowest level ever against the dollar and sterling, after being spared a possible interest rate hike late Friday.

All eyes will be fixed on the currency after it plunged to below 4.60 on the dollar for the first time on Friday, hit by a wave of speculative selling from foreign investors and downbeat comments from Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals.
That took the government bond market to its lowest level in nearly five months and prompted heavy selling of the currency, particularly by overseas investors, dealers said.

Stals warned that already high interest rates might have to be raised further if there was no slowdown in money supply and credit growth, and cautioned that the country's low reserves ruled out any early scrapping of exchange controls on residents.

Traders said the bond market was seen strengthening on Monday to around the 15.67 percent level if money supply data came in as expected. Close on the heels of its release, long bonds were off their worst levels.
There are no major economic indicators due this week.

Elsewhere, the world's most closely watched economic indicator will hog the limelight on Friday when October non-farm payroll figures cap a prolific week for U.S. data only four days before the presidential election.

Neil Mackinnon, chief economist at Citibank, said October payrolls growth was likely to exceed 200,000 and the September figure might be revised up. He described the September data as an aberration due to special factors on teacher employment.
Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Markets, said the payrolls number was part of a deluge of U.S. data whose other highlights include third quarter GDP figures due on Wednesday.
They also include, and personal income and spending data for September on Thursday.
GDP grew 4.7 percent in the second quarter and Wattret said he was looking for the new figure to come in at 2.25 percent.

In Europe, analysts said guessing games over the Bundesbank's intentions on interest rates might continue because it suited the German central bank to keep markets on their toes by feeding them ambiguous comments.
Elsewhere in Europe, analysts saw scope for some interest rate cuts following those seen this week in Italy and Sweden.
Wattret said further cuts in Italy were still one or two months away because the central bank did not want to give the impression of slashing rates too quickly.
However, he said one possibility was that France might trim five to 10 basis points off its five to 10 day rate if the French franc stayed strong.

Any cut, Wattrett said, would certainly be portrayed as being in response to the strength of the currency rather than an expected further deterioration in France's 12.6 percent unemployment rate when September data are released on Thursday.

Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at BankAmerica, noted a US quarterly refunding release Wednesday. "People will be looking for an increase in participation coming out of Japan which should lead to additional downside pressure on the yen."

In Britain, Hawkins said the purchasing managers survey and consumer credit data were expected to fit in with the view that the economy was accelerating, leading to speculation that interest rates might have to rise before the 1997 election.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would turn down any rate hike request from Bank of England governor Eddie George when the two have their monthly meeting on Wednesday, Hawkins added.
